phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.prompt: A supervisor wants a file note after a first coaching talk about three late clock-ins this month. What should the note contain?

options.a: The late dates, the start-time rule, and a dated follow-up to check attendance
options.b: A judgment that the employee has a bad attitude and is not a team player
options.c: A final warning issued today so the file shows the issue was treated as severe
options.d: A private manager memo stored at home that the employee is not allowed to see

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.explanation: Early coaching notes should stick to observable facts: which shifts were late, the attendance expectation, and when the manager will check again. That record supports later steps if the pattern continues and is fair if the employee asks to see it. Attitude labels, jumping to a final warning, and secret side files all weaken the documentation.

distractorExplanations.b: Personality and attitude labels are not observable conduct; they read as bias and are hard to defend if the note is later used in discipline.
distractorExplanations.c: A first coaching talk is an early step; a final warning skips progressive discipline unless the conduct is already egregious.
distractorExplanations.d: The employee should know what was discussed and expected; a hidden home file undercuts due process and discovery later.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.prompt: Camera footage shows a picker punch a coworker after an argument. The handbook lists workplace violence as immediate-discharge conduct. What should HR recommend?

options.a: Give a first verbal warning because the picker has no prior write-ups on file
options.b: Move to summary discharge under the violence rule rather than more coaching steps
options.c: Write two attendance warnings first so the packet looks like progressive discipline
options.d: Pause all discipline because the picker emailed an overtime complaint yesterday

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.explanation: Progressive steps can be skipped when the conduct is egregious and the published policy allows summary action. Workplace violence is the classic example: the file still needs a prompt, documented investigation, but HR does not have to coach first. Inventing unrelated warnings or freezing action because of a recent complaint creates other legal problems.

distractorExplanations.a: A clean prior record does not force a verbal warning when policy treats violence as summary-discharge conduct.
distractorExplanations.c: Padding the file with unrelated attendance write-ups is dishonest documentation and does not cure an investigation gap.
distractorExplanations.d: A recent complaint is not a reason to skip or stall violence discipline; rushing because of the complaint would raise retaliation risk, but the violence still must be addressed on its facts.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.prompt: A union assembler in a private plant is called in about missing kits that may lead to a write-up and asks for a steward. What should the supervisor do?

options.a: Refuse the steward, because Weingarten applies only at NLRB unfair-labor-practice hearings
options.b: Let the assembler bring a personal lawyer instead of waiting for a union representative
options.c: Pause the interview until a steward can attend; this is an investigatory meeting
options.d: Bring a steward only for a routine start-of-shift huddle, which is not investigatory

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.explanation: Weingarten rights (private-sector union settings) let an employee request a union representative in an investigatory interview the employee reasonably believes may lead to discipline. The operational move is to wait for a steward or stop the interview; the employer may not compel the interview without the representative once the request is made.

distractorExplanations.a: Weingarten is about the employer's investigatory interview, not a hearing at the NLRB.
distractorExplanations.b: The right is to a union representative, not a personal attorney; swapping in counsel does not satisfy Weingarten.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine operational huddles are not Weingarten events; the right attaches when discipline is a reasonable prospect.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.prompt: An employee reports a site manager's repeated sexual comments. Who should run the investigation and how?

options.a: Wait for a second reporter so HR can show a pattern before any interviews start
options.b: Have the site manager investigate, because they already know the workgroup
options.c: Promise the reporter that their name will never be shared with anyone
options.d: Assign an impartial investigator promptly and keep a contemporaneous record

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-01.explanation: Harassment complaints require a prompt, impartial, documented investigation. The accused supervisor cannot run it. Employers act on the first report; waiting for a pattern undermines the Faragher/Ellerth defense. Confidentiality is limited to a need-to-know circle, so a promise of total secrecy is not available.

distractorExplanations.a: The first complaint is enough to open a file; waiting for a second reporter delays correction and weakens the employer's defense.
distractorExplanations.b: The accused manager has a conflict of interest; an investigator must be outside that reporting line.
distractorExplanations.c: Investigators can limit gossip, but they cannot promise that the reporter's identity will never be known to witnesses or the accused.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: A store director wants to fire an at-will cashier the day after the cashier filed an EEOC charge, saying the store is at-will. What should HR say?

options.a: Do not fire for that reason; at-will does not cover discrimination or retaliation
options.b: Proceed today; at-will status means no reason is required even after a charge
options.c: Demote instead of firing so the charge has no effect on the personnel file
options.d: Fire and backfill this week so the pending charge can be treated as closed

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: At-will employment lets most private employers end the relationship without cause, but it does not legalize a discriminatory or retaliatory motive. Timing a discharge to an EEOC filing is a classic retaliation fact pattern. HR should separate any independent performance case from the protected activity and keep the file clean.

distractorExplanations.b: At-will does not wipe out Title VII or retaliation rules; a charge is protected activity even if no written reason is otherwise required.
distractorExplanations.c: A demotion tied to the charge is still an adverse action and can support the same retaliation claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Backfilling does not moot a charge; it can look like the employer is covering its tracks.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: A second documented lockout-tagout miss occurred. Operations wants one more chance before discharge. Which tool should HR use?

options.a: A hallway verbal reminder with a handshake and no written terms or dates
options.b: A last-chance agreement that states the next like violation ends employment
options.c: A severance-and-release packet the employee signs while still on the job
options.d: A development plan that says further misses will have no job consequence

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: A last-chance agreement is a written final boundary: the rule, the remaining period, and that a further like violation ends employment. It is used when operations will retain the employee one more time. Verbal-only reminders, severance packets while still employed, and plans with no consequence do not create that boundary.

distractorExplanations.a: A hallway verbal is an early coaching step, not a documented last chance before termination.
distractorExplanations.c: Severance-and-release belongs at separation; it is not a tool for keeping someone employed on strict terms.
distractorExplanations.d: If the plan says there is no consequence, it cannot function as a last chance and confuses later discharge.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: After a pulse drop, a director wants skip-level coffees with every individual contributor. How should HR design them?

options.a: Treat skip-levels as the official grievance path and close the handbook process
options.b: Cancel weekly one-on-ones with the immediate supervisor during the skip-level month
options.c: Keep every note in the director's drawer and do not share themes with HR partners
options.d: Use them to hear themes while routing formal complaints through published policy

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: Skip-levels are a listening tool: they can surface engagement issues without replacing the manager or the complaint procedure. Formal grievances and harassment reports still follow the published path. Themes should be shared with HR so patterns get action, and direct-manager one-on-ones stay in place.

distractorExplanations.a: Skip-levels are not a substitute grievance procedure; closing the handbook path creates inconsistent due process.
distractorExplanations.b: Canceling the supervisor's one-on-ones undercuts the manager the skip-level is supposed to complement.
distractorExplanations.c: Parking themes with one leader hides patterns HR needs for investigations, engagement work, and risk.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: A CBA sets a three-step grievance. A supervisor wants to skip to an open-door with the plant VP. What should HR do?

options.a: Use the open-door path because it is faster than following the contract steps
options.b: File an NLRB unfair-labor-practice charge instead of using the grievance
options.c: Stay on the CBA grievance steps; do not substitute a management-designed appeal
options.d: Let the supervisor write a one-step appeal because they own the employee handbook

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: In a union shop the contractual grievance procedure is the bargained path for contract disputes. Supervisors do not freelance an open-door or handbook appeal that skips steps. NLRB unfair-labor-practice charges address statutory NLRA violations; they are not the substitute for a CBA grievance on a contract issue.

distractorExplanations.a: Speed does not authorize bypassing bargained steps; the open-door is a non-union tool.
distractorExplanations.b: A ULP charge goes to the NLRB for alleged NLRA violations, not as a shortcut around the contract grievance.
distractorExplanations.d: Management cannot replace the CBA procedure with a handbook appeal the supervisor invents.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: Pulse scores fell on 'I can raise concerns.' Leaders want the number up before the next survey. What should HR do first?

options.a: Choose a few drivers, take visible action, and close the loop with employees
options.b: Pay every manager a bonus solely for a five-point jump on that survey item
options.c: Field a weekly pulse until the score moves, then drop all follow-up talk
options.d: Post the scores in the newsletter and wait for the next annual survey cycle

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: Engagement surveys create value when leaders pick a short list of drivers, act, and tell employees what changed. Publishing scores with no action, surveying more often without follow-through, and paying for the number all teach people to game or ignore the instrument.

distractorExplanations.b: Bonuses tied only to the score invite pressure on respondents and gaming rather than fixing the concern-raising climate.
distractorExplanations.c: Weekly pulses without action add survey fatigue; dropping communication after the number moves repeats the cynicism cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing results and waiting a year is the classic 'survey to nowhere' that lowers trust on the next pulse.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: Two peers begin dating; six months later one is promoted into the other's reporting line. What is the romance policy meant to do?

options.a: Forbid dating between any two employees anywhere in the company, including peers
options.b: Manage conflict and harassment risk through disclosure and a reporting-line change
options.c: Replace annual harassment training now that dating is addressed in a written rule
options.d: Require HR to approve social dates before employees may see each other off-site

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: Workplace-relationship policies are risk tools: they catch supervisor-subordinate conflicts, require disclosure, and usually force a reporting-line or transfer change. They do not typically ban all peer dating, pre-clear social lives, or replace harassment training. PHR work is to administer disclosure and the conflict fix consistently.

distractorExplanations.a: Blanket bans on all peer relationships are hard to enforce and raise privacy issues; the usual trigger is a reporting line.
distractorExplanations.c: A romance rule complements harassment training; it does not satisfy the training obligation.
distractorExplanations.d: Most policies require disclosure of a reporting-line relationship, not prior HR approval of off-site dating.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: After a manager restates a lawful, safe weekend coverage order, a technician says they will not do it and walks out. How should HR classify this?

options.a: Ordinary staff-meeting disagreement that should not be written into the file
options.b: A protected OSHA refusal because weekend work is treated as imminent danger
options.c: A missed-deadline performance issue rather than a refusal of a stated directive
options.d: Insubordination: refusing a lawful, safe order after the manager restated it

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: Insubordination is a clear refusal of a lawful, reasonably safe work order after it has been stated. Weekend coverage that is not an OSHA imminent-danger situation fits. Respectful debate in a meeting and ordinary missed deadlines are different problems and should not be labeled insubordination.

distractorExplanations.a: Walking out after a restated order is a refusal, not mere disagreement in a meeting.
distractorExplanations.b: OSHA protects refusal of work that poses a real imminent danger; a lawful weekend queue is not that exception.
distractorExplanations.c: A missed deadline is performance; this employee refused the assignment itself.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: HR sits in on a 12-person layoff meeting at a WARN-covered site. What must the meeting script include?

options.a: The business reason, last day, and any WARN or benefits information that applies
options.b: A WARN notice handed to each person as they walk out of the conference room today
options.c: An unscripted promise of rehire priority so the conversation stays calm and short
options.d: An OWBPA waiver that gives employees age 40+ only seven days to consider a group deal

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: A RIF conversation should state the business reason, the effective date, and the benefits, severance, and WARN pieces that actually apply. Covered WARN events need 60 days' advance notice, not a packet on the walk-out. OWBPA group programs give employees 40+ 45 days to consider and 7 days to revoke, not 7 days to consider.

distractorExplanations.b: WARN, when it applies, is 60 days' advance notice for a covered layoff, not same-day delivery in the meeting.
distractorExplanations.c: Casual rehire promises can create contract claims; stick to the documented reason and written benefits.
distractorExplanations.d: Seven days is the OWBPA revocation window, not the consideration period for a group program (45 days).

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: A vendor offers peer mediation for workplace conflict. Which case should HR keep out of mediation and send to investigation?

options.a: Two coworkers who clash over the tone of a missed status email
options.b: A report of sexual harassment or a threat of physical violence
options.c: Peers arguing over who will cover a Saturday overtime shift
options.d: A mild style clash about how weekly team huddles are run

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: Peer mediation can help style clashes, email tone, and shift-swap disputes between equals. Harassment and violence are not mediate-and-compromise problems: they need a prompt investigation, possible separation of the parties, and discipline if substantiated. Putting those complaints into mediation can look like the employer failed to act.

distractorExplanations.a: Email-tone friction between peers is a typical mediation fit, not a substitute for a harassment investigation.
distractorExplanations.c: Scheduling disputes between peers are a common, appropriate mediation topic when no policy violation is alleged.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild style differences are the core use case for mediation; they do not require a formal misconduct investigation.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.prompt: A no-fault attendance policy assigns the same point for certified FMLA leave as for a no-call no-show. What should HR change?

options.a: Keep the points; identical treatment is the purpose of a no-fault system
options.b: Point tardies only and stop assessing unexcused full-day absences
options.c: Drop the call-in rule for everyone because FMLA users cannot be required to call
options.d: Exclude protected FMLA, ADA, and USERRA time from the point assessments

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-02.explanation: No-fault point systems fail when they treat protected leave like unprotected absence. FMLA, ADA reasonable-leave, and USERRA absences generally cannot draw the same points as a no-call no-show. Unexcused tardies and absences can still be pointed, and usual call-in procedures may still apply to FMLA users.

distractorExplanations.a: Consistency is not a defense when the points attach to legally protected leave; that design is the failure mode.
distractorExplanations.b: Pointing unexcused full-day absences is ordinary; the illegal piece is pointing certified protected leave.
distractorExplanations.c: Employers may still require FMLA users to follow usual call-in rules; dropping call-in for everyone is not required.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-03.prompt: An employee emails that they resign Friday. The supervisor wants badge access left on until the paycheck two weeks later. What should HR do?

options.a: Reject the resignation until the employee provides two weeks of written notice
options.b: Recode the separation as a for-cause firing so unemployment can be blocked
options.c: Confirm Friday as the last day in writing and cut systems access that same day
options.d: Accept the notice only verbally and leave badge access on through payday two weeks out

phr-hrci-readiness-check-employee-rel-03.explanation: Treat a clear resignation as a resignation: confirm last day in writing, collect access on that date, and run the normal offboarding checklist. Two weeks' notice is a courtesy, not a condition of acceptance. Leaving access open until payday and recoding the event as a for-cause firing both create security and legal risk.

distractorExplanations.a: At-will employees can resign without two weeks' notice; HR cannot hold the person until a longer notice appears.
distractorExplanations.b: Relabeling a quit as a for-cause termination without facts is inaccurate and can support a claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Verbal-only acceptance leaves the last day fuzzy, and access should end on the last day, not on payday.
